fullText:
For more than four decades, the investing world operated on a foundational assumption: that a portfolio consisting of 60% stocks and 40% bonds would protect you when markets turned. For roughly the past 20 years, a second assumption took hold alongside it: that a handful of dominant tech companies would keep growing into whatever price investors were willing to pay. This has taken on several shapes, with the FAANG companies morphing into the "Magnificent Seven" during the pandemic, and the AI boom crowning a new group of "hyperscalers."

But these assumptions are taking a hit from sources that rarely deliver bad news about the markets they cover.

Goldman Sachs, one of the Street's most consistently bullish research shops, published a note Monday authored by chief global equity strategist Peter Oppenheimer conceding that "there does not appear to be a valuation bubble, but there may be an earnings bubble" in the technology sector.

The same day, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in his Daily Spark note that "the 60/40 portfolio is broken," arguing that with the AI trade slowing down and government debt projected to reach 175% of GDP, "neither the 60 nor the 40 responds to what made it work in the first place."

Both notes came after a week of Big Tech earnings that saw shockingly large moves both up and down for major tech firms, with analysts debating whether they reflected the true shape of the AI moat or "financial nihilism."

Microsoft made history with a 17% stock surge, adding nearly $500 billion in market capitalization in one day, its largest single-day move since the financial crisis year of 2008. In fact, Oppenheimer said Monday that the market is seeing things change in a way they haven't since the Great Recession.

The 60/40 rule wasn't always gospel. Its theoretical roots trace to Harry Markowitz's 1952 work on portfolio theory, but it only became institutional orthodoxy during the four-decade stretch of falling interest rates that began in the early 1980s. That decline let bonds do double duty as both income and ballast against equities, a dynamic that market analysts have called the "golden age" of investing.

Slok's warning isn't a reaction to one bad earnings season. He has argued since at least 2023 that rates would stay "higher for longer" than consensus expected. By late May 2026, he had sharpened that macro call into a specific yield-curve mechanism: Front-end rates were rising on sticky inflation; the middle of the curve was under pressure "because of hyperscaler issuance"; and long-end rates were climbing on "more Treasury supply and less Fed demand." His Aug. 3 argument that "the real risk emerges if the AI trade reverses or markets become more worried about government deficits" is a continuation of that multiyear thesis, not a new one.

title: Top Dem torches socialists taking over his party: 'They're anti-American'
description: Josh Gottheimer says Democratic Socialists of America are "not Democrats" and accuses them of trying to hijack the party as a vessel for socialism.
fullText:
A leading House Democrat went scorched-earth on insurgent socialists rising within his party, repeatedly telling them to start their own party and accusing them of trying to "hijack" the Democratic Party as a "vessel" for their communist, "anti-American," open-border platform.

House Intelligence Committee member Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., a leader of the moderate Blue Dog Coalition, told Fox News on Sunday that the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is "not Democrats" and rejected the idea that its platform is compatible with the Democratic Party's.

"Obviously, I'm a very proud, commonsense Democrat, and I don't think DSA members are Democrats. They're socialists, right? And I'm all for them having their own party if they want one, but if they're trying to take over our party, that's unacceptable to me," Gottheimer said on "The Big Weekend Show."

Dem Rep Henry Cuellar Rejects Dsa Agenda, Says Socialists Are Trying To 'Use' Democratic Party

"Their values, their ideas are certainly not in line with ours, and they don't support our leadership. They're trying to use the Democratic Party as a vessel for their ideas. And as you heard in some of these conventions, literally, they're supporting the Communist Manifesto and [Leon] Trotsky, they're anti-American, they are anti-cop, they don't believe in borders."

Gottheimer was referring to man-on-the-street clips of DSA members at the group's Chicago convention. One socialist said they are organizing a front to get "ICE off our campuses," while a member of the DSA's National Political Committee said people such as Gottheimer who call them anti-American do not understand that their platform is the "most American thing you can do."

Another DSA NPC member said socialism is the "same kind of stuff that I am used to [in] growing up in the Christian Church."

Democratic Socialists Of America Activists Signed Pledge To Support, Defend 'Chinese Socialism'

Gottheimer said 45 million voters are registered Democrats, compared with 150,000 official DSA members.

"They're not welcome in the Democratic Party," he said.

He pushed back against members of his own party who have expressed openness to DSA-aligned candidates such as Maine oysterman Graham Platner.

Graham Platner Blames Nazi Tattoo On Military 'Culture,' Draws Backlash From Gop Veterans

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., who represents Silicon Valley, said Democrats should not have "watched wealth pile up on Wall Street and Silicon Valley" at the expense of working-class Americans, adding that "the Democratic Party needs reform."

Gottheimer countered that fringe coalitions are mounting insurgencies in both parties and "trying to barge in" with incompatible ideas.

He also pointed to longtime Clinton confidant James Carville, who told Fox News that he would disown the Democratic Party if left-wing streamer Hasan Piker were permitted to become one of its leaders.

Former U.S. Marine Corps bomb technician Johnny Joey Jones asked whether Gottheimer would also leave the party over Piker or if Democratic leaders embraced socialists such as Harlem's Darializa Chevalier.

"Well, [House Minority Leader Hakeem] Jeffries won't — and let me be very clear that Hasan Piker is not a Democrat – the guy is the ultimate grifter, right? He's the guy who said that 9/11 is America's fault… We've got to make it clear he's not welcome in the Democratic Party."

Gottheimer said the DSA platform shows that the organization is incompatible with the Democratic Party. He added that socialists can "scream and yell and try to …hijack [the party] and shove their ideas in and use it as a vessel."

"We have to make clear that's not who we are…"

While Gottheimer reiterated that he does not plan to leave the Democratic Party any time soon, Jones noted that one prominent New Jersey Democrat already has.

Rep. Jeff Van Drew, whose district includes Cape May, switched parties during President Donald Trump's first term, angering South Jersey Democratic committees as the longtime lawmaker embraced Trump's platform.

"You wouldn't be the first New Jersey congressman to find a better party. I'm just saying leave the door open if you want to," Jones said.

Gottheimer's district includes liberal New York City suburbs immediately west of the George Washington Bridge and the deep-red, Trump-friendly Skylands near the Delaware Water Gap, making it one of the most politically diverse districts in the state's congressional delegation.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA and Piker for comment.

title: Analysis: Trump fumes as top allies back down on his personal battles
description: A president used to bending US politics to his will faces two stinging losses in a matter of days, writes the BBC's Anthony Zurcher.
fullText:
Watch: "She folded like an umbrella" - Trump attacks Jeanine Pirro over Reflecting Pool

It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.

In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term.

From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making.

Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of contravening evidence.

Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him.

"The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior.

Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted – what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury – provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it.

Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday.

"She folded like an umbrella," he groused.

If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him.

'She folded like an umbrella' - Trump slams Jeanine Pirro over Reflecting Pool case

Trump administration drops Reflecting Pool vandalism charge and admits 'botched' repairs

One of Trump's closest allies – his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche – was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis.

Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination. They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution.

Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.

Holdout senators back Blanche for AG after he formally withdraws Trump fund plan

In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund.

"It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go.

The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns.

In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said.

Trump on Blanche: "He's going to do a great job"

While the Reflecting Pool prosecution and the so-called "anti-weaponisation fund" may be topics of intense presidential interest, they barely register as concerns for the larger American public.

That is decidedly not the case with the war with Iran, where Trump is once again accusing Iran of deceit amid another round of on-again, off-again negotiations and threats of overwhelming American military action.

On Monday, after asserting the previous day that he had called off "an attack that would have been the biggest attack since World War II" at the behest of Iranian officials and Arab intermediaries, Trump took to Truth Social to condemn what he said was Iranian duplicity after Iran denied any new direct negotiations.

"They ask for a meeting, some would say 'beg', talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they're not having any discussions," Trump wrote.

If Iranians are misrepresenting the status of talks it wouldn't be the first time – but it also wouldn't be the first time Trump has seemingly taken their assurances at face value and heralded a new diplomatic breakthrough.

The latest twists in the war have become a familiar pattern with little progress, as polls continue to show American disapproval of the conflict and concern that Trump is not achieving his war goals.

Those recent public-opinion surveys suggest the war has become a growing drag on the president's overall popularity. A recent Associated Press poll puts Trump's approval at 33%, aligned with similar findings by CNN, Quinnipiac and YouGov. That matches or is below Trump's ratings after the Capitol riot and is above only Richard Nixon – who resigned from office in disgrace - among second-term US presidents in modern American history.

Trump, however, has repeatedly dismissed surveys suggesting his historic unpopularity.

"My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been," he posted to Truth Social on Monday.

In three months, voters will head to the polls for congressional midterm elections. And Trump has shown surprising strength at the ballot box in the past, even in the face of seemingly daunting poll numbers.

While Trump may be grappling with – and, at times denying - recent adversity, that will be ultimate measure of his political fate. And if Republicans struggle, it may provide yet another reality that Trump, despite his best efforts, must eventially face.

title: What we know about the In-N-Out Burger shooting suspect
description: The suspect, Chad Williams, died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
fullText:
Some details are emerging about the man suspected of opening fire outside an In-N-Out Burger location in Idaho over the weekend, killing three people, as a motive in the mass shooting remains under investigation.

The suspect in Saturday's shooting -- 24-year-old Chad Williams -- died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound after police say he opened fire near a busy shopping area in Twin Falls.

Williams attended the College of Southern Idaho in 2022 and 2023 but did not graduate with a degree, a college spokesperson told ABC News.

He was a senator in the college's student government, the spokesperson confirmed, until he was impeached from that role in February 2023.

Elijah Moseley, who served on the school's student government at the time, told ABC Boise affiliate KIVI the impeachment was "procedural" and that they were freeing up a seat for someone who was more engaged.

Moseley told the station that he and Williams fell out of touch in the years since, calling the news of the shooting "shocking."

The Twin Falls Police Department said investigators are "confident" the suspect acted alone.

Three people were killed and seven others injured, some critically, in the shooting, police said. An In-N-Out employee was among those killed, the company confirmed.

An armed off-duty Idaho state trooper and a private citizen confronted the shooter, likely driving him from the scene and avoiding further casualties, according to Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks.

3 killed, 7 injured in shooting at In-N-Out in Idaho, police say

A motive for the shooting remains under investigation. Hicks said the suspected gunman's family members are cooperating with the investigation.

Police were still interviewing witnesses and asked anyone with information to come forward in the wake of the shooting.

The FBI said it was aware of the situation and was offering assistance to local law enforcement, according to an agency spokesman. The agency also asked people to submit any video, audio or still images that may have captured the shooting.

title: US State Department to close consulates in Canada, Japan and Indonesia, sources say
description: The U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 3 (Reuters) - The U.S. State Department has notified Congress that it plans to close five foreign missions in a rare downsizing of America's global diplomatic footprint, according ‌to people familiar with the notice.

In the notice sent to some congressional committees late last week, the State ‌Department said it planned to close its posts in St. George's, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada. The people familiar with ​the notice spoke on the condition of anonymity because the notice was not public.

The expected closures, which have not been previously reported, represent a rare example of the U.S. closing multiple foreign missions in a downsizing that is not tied to a particular geopolitical event.

Early last year, during the opening months of the Trump administration, the State Department began preparations to shut down nearly ‌a dozen foreign missions, Reuters and other ⁠media outlets reported at the time, as part of a broader push by the Republican president to transform the U.S. bureaucracy so that it is fully aligned with his "America First" agenda.

The ⁠White House Office of Management and Budget had advocated for an even more ambitious closure program, targeting up to 30 foreign missions. Some administration officials have privately argued that some smaller foreign missions are inessential and not cost effective.

Democrats and some former foreign policy ​and national ​security officials argue that cuts to the U.S. diplomatic footprint - coupled ​with the dismantling of the U.S. Agency for ‌International Development, which provided billions of dollars worth of aid globally - risks undermining American leadership, while leaving a dangerous vacuum for adversaries like China and Russia to fill.

While the State Department did undergo a broad bureaucratic overhaul last year – cutting dozens of bureaus and hundreds of staff – no foreign missions were shuttered.

Asked for comment on Sunday, the State Department issued a statement that did not confirm the closures but said it was focused on ensuring that the nation's diplomatic footprint was efficient ‌and effective. The department added that it was committed to following ​congressional notification procedures.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has portrayed cost-cutting measures as ​necessary to right-size an organization many conservatives see as ​bloated and overly bureaucratic.

The U.S. mission in St. George's, Grenada, is an embassy. The posts in ‌Medan, Winnipeg and Nagoya are consulates, while the ​post in Douala is an "embassy branch ​office." Consulates and branch offices typically represent U.S. interests in regions outside a foreign country's capital city, where the U.S. embassy is typically located.

During the administration of former President Joe Biden, the U.S. government opened several foreign ​missions, all of them in the ‌Pacific region, where the U.S. is competing for influence with China.

While China does not have a functioning foreign ​mission in Douala or Winnipeg, it does have a diplomatic presence in St. George's, Nagoya and Medan.

(Reporting ​by Humeyra Pamuk and Gram Slattery; Editing by Stephen Coates)

title: Google Never Should Have Put Nano Banana Into Google Earth in the First Place
description: Why is Google Earth intentionally messing with reality?
fullText:
Last week, Google rolled out its AI image generation model, Nano Banana 2, to Google Earth, its world explorer program. The company advertised the integration as a way for people to create infographics about different locations around the globe, or to generate historical landscapes of modern-day imagery. Users were also invited to generate their "dream homes" against real-world backdrops—so if you had plans to build an extension on your home, or visions of a vacation house on the lake, you could visualize it with Nano Banana 2 in Google Earth.

The news followed a trend of Google integrating its AI platforms into just about every one of its products and services (for example, last week it added new Gemini capabilities to Google Docs for Workspace users). From the company's perspective, it likely made total sense to add Nano Banana 2 to Google Earth. As it turned out, however, this is one product that Gemini wasn't meant for.

Just one day after Google launched this big Nano Banana 2 integration, it rolled it back. The company issued an update to its original announcement, which read: "We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world. We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes; however, we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails. It's important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI-generated."

This statement doesn't properly describe the images that users were generating with this tool. In my view, it went beyond "violating" Google's policies: The internet, predictably, used Nano Banana 2 to generate inappropriate and insensitive images based on real locations. Perhaps it won't come as a surprise to learn that one of the images that took off most was of a plane crashing into the new World Trade Center in Manhattan. Other images depicted the Eiffel Tower destroyed, or the Egyptian pyramids collapsing into a sinkhole. While many would likely understand these were produced in jest, plenty more could see these "official" Google Earth images online and assume the worst.

But beyond the jokes, the potential for misinformation and disinformation was alarming. For example, one user demonstrated how they used the tool to place refugees shoulder to shoulder near the Mexican border. One could imagine such an image going viral, with viewers tricked into thinking the Google Earth still was an actual satellite image. Google likely has some guardrails in place preventing many image generations from taking place, but clearly those limitations weren't strong enough. And since anyone, whether they paid for Google's AI features or not, could use Nano Banana 2 with Google Earth, all one had to do was open Google Earth and fiddle with a malicious prompt until Nano Banana 2 complied.

It doesn't take an AI skeptic to explain why this was a bad idea in the first place—but then again, few AI companies seem to be employing any skepticism before jamming generative AI features into their products. Tools like Google Earth are meant to be educational. You use them to learn about the world, its geography, and what different cities and landscapes look like. I personally love spending time spinning the digital globe around to learn about a new location, and often drop a pin on a random spot to see what it looks like on Street View. The reason I do this is that I understand Google Earth to be an accurate, reliable look at the world; if that weren't the case, why would I bother?

As such, it makes no sense to me for Google to introduce a tool that, by necessity, generates inaccurate and false views of the world. One of its selling points was viewing a place on the map as it looked in the past, but that's not what Nano Banana 2 was doing. Instead, the AI would pull from its training data to generate what it thought a historical representation of the area in question would be. If you asked it to show you what Paris looked like in 1726, it would likely overlay generic buildings and structures onto the map, rather than depict what Paris actually looked like three hundred years ago. What you're getting is the illusion of history; entertaining, perhaps, but certainly not educational—no better than scrolling through AI history slop on social media.

The same goes for the AI's "infographics." Companies like Google love to tout AI's potential as an educational tool, and on the surface, it seems like a great thing for Google Earth to generate learning graphics to teach you about a location on the map. But your generated graphic isn't vetted by anyone, and definitely not by an expert: The image that Nano Banana 2 spits out could be full of half-truths and hallucinations, and, what's worse, it won't offer any sources you can click through to check the AI's work. Casual users may retain the information they "learn" from these infographics, whether that data is correct or not.

At its worst, this feature was a disinformation machine. If you wanted to convince people that something bad happened in a particular part of the world, you could just type your request in, and Nano Banana 2 could spit out a realistic satellite image of your idea for easy sharing on social media. At a time when AI is spreading misinformation at a rapid rate, this only pours fuel onto an already raging fire. Companies like Google should be looking for ways to separate AI slop from real information, not helping it grow.

This isn't an argument against AI tools in their entirety, but it is an argument against embedding generative AI into an educational tool. What utility Google believes AI serves by taking truth and clouding it in falsehoods I do not know—other than giving it yet another example it can point to in order to tout its AI "success."

title: How to Finally Sync Your Fitbit Data to Apple Health
description: This is major news for Fitbit fans.
fullText:
While Fitbits are a favorite option for go-to fitness trackers—they're thin, unobtrusive, and cheap—its app, Google Health, has always had its problems. However, things might be turning around. The Google Health app has finally received an update that lets it send data to Apple Health.

Google Health (formerly known as the Fitbit app) could always pull in fitness, sleep, and wellness stats directly from devices like Fitbit trackers. However, Fitbit devices have historically lacked any built-in way to sync directly with Apple Health. To get around that limitation, anyone who wanted their data to flow both ways had to turn to third-party tools or manual workarounds. This latest Google Health update finally allows metrics like step counts, distance, heart rate, and sleep data to flow into Apple's health platform, too. This means the metrics on your phone will more seamlessly reflect what your Fitbit has been tracking.

To start syncing your Fitbit data to Apple Health, you'll first need to update your Google Health app. Open the Apple App Store, go to your updates list, and select Update next to the app. Once you have the latest version downloaded, open the Google Health app, tap "Connections" in the top left, select "Apps and services," and then add Apple Health. If you don't see the syncing option right away, try closing and refreshing the app.

Unfortunately, as of this writing, the update isn't perfect: Some users on Reddit have pointed out that certain metrics, like heart rate variability, aren't included in the transfer—or at least, not yet. Time will tell if another update fixes these missing metrics. And if missing HRV stats is a dealbreaker for you, check out the iPhone app Bevel, which can be a decent all-around replacement for the Google Health app.

fullText:
Mixed martial arts fighter Allan Nascimento has died at the age of 34, says the UFC.

According to MMA's leading promotion, the Brazilian flyweight was found unresponsive on Monday morning after suffering an apparent heart attack in his sleep.

"Despite the efforts of the responding medical team, he was pronounced deceased at the scene," added a UFC statement., external

"Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Allan's family, friends, team-mates and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time."

Nascimento had been with the UFC since 2021 and his last fight was a split-decision loss to Mitch Raposo in June.

That left Nascimento with an overall MMA record of 22 wins and seven losses, with a 4-2 record in the UFC.

title: Fulham sign Garcia and Palacios from Real Madrid
description: Fulham sign Gonzalo Garcia and Cesar Palacios from Real Madrid on five-year deals.
fullText:
Fulham have signed Gonzalo Garcia and Cesar Palacios from Real Madrid on five-year deals.

Garcia, 22, made 39 appearances for the Spanish giants last term, scoring eight goals in all competitions.

The forward, who won his first cap for Spain in June, will reunite with new Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa, for a reported fee of around £34m, with the pair having worked together at the Bernabeu.

"I'm very grateful, very happy to be here," Garcia said.

"I have to thank the board and Arbeloa for the trust they've put in me, and I'm very, very excited to start."

The highly rated striker, joint-top scorer at the Club World Cup last summer, will be joined at Craven Cottage by former Real team-mate Palacios.

The 21-year-old attacking midfielder also arrives on a contract that runs until the summer of 2031, although the club has the option to extend the agreements for both players by a further 12 months.

Palacios made five appearances for Real's senior side - all from the substitutes bench - and has played for Spain at under-20 level.

title: Tierney shows value as Celtic title defence begins
description: BBC Scotland looks at the impact of Kieran Tierney in Celtic's win over Dundee in the Scottish Premiership.
fullText:
On a tough night at the very start of a new season, against a dogged Dundee, it was a familiar name that helped Celtic usher in victory.

No, not Benjamin Nygren - last season's top scorer and the man who nodded in the winner to kickstart the Scottish Premiership defence - but Kieran Tierney, the man who crossed the ball for the Swede to head in.

The left-back has arguably been Celtic's best player since the return of Martin O'Neill in January, but his renaissance has gone a little under the radar.

Perhaps that's because we expect so much from the man who once fetched Celtic a reported £25m in a move to Arsenal.

Regardless, he still registered 12 assists last season, the most of any Celtic player, and scored six goals from defence.

One of O'Neill's most trusted lieutenants, he's contracted until 2030 but reports have suggested a potential return to Spain, so just how important is he to Celtic?

Sportsound: Reaction as Celtic kick-off their title defence with a narrow win over Dundee

Despite Kasper Hogh's 0.88 expected goals (xG), it was actually Tierney who had the most shots on target for Celtic against Dundee - albeit only two.

He created more chances than any of his team-mates (four) and sent in eight crosses, the most of any Celtic player.

"He looked like old Kieran Tierney. He was bombing forward, getting in the box, had a couple shots on goal, doing all his defensive stuff, he was excellent," said BBC Scotland's chief sports writer Tom English.

Excellent was the word to describe the left-back's cross to Nygren, and it was just what Celtic needed.

In the first half, the reigning champions were pushed hard by a Dundee side that set out to be aggressive and frustrate the hosts, and that's just what they did.

But the chances started to become more frequent, and soon it was the trusty left boot of Tierney that unlocked the door, allowing Nygren to head home from six yards out with a pinpoint cross.

However, his impact on this Celtic team is nothing new.

Only Falkirk's Calvin Miller, now at Hearts, registered more assists last season. At Celtic, only Daizen Maeda created more big chances - 14 to Tierney's 12.

Defensively, he consistently shows up as one of the best defenders in the league for his contributions, his tackling, clearances, blocking shots.

And for all the talk of managing his minutes, only three full-backs across the league played more than Tierney. That said, he played the full game on only 10 occasions in the league.

"Those players are the football club," manager O'Neill said of Tierney and captain Callum McGregor. "They are the backbone of Celtic, and I'm delighted to have them."

With last season's on-loan left-back Marcelo Sarrachi having returned to his parent club Boca Juniors, there's currently no other senior left-backs on Celtic's books.

"Of course [it's important to bring in cover for Tierney], that's something we're looking at," O'Neill told BBC Scotland.

"Kieran, with the best will in the world, will not get through every single game. Last year, he was recovering and didn't see some games out because he puts so much into it. We're looking that way."

It was reported today that Osasuna have enquired about Tierney, although that same article suggested Celtic chiefs will knock back any offers for the 29-year-old.

Given the lack of options in that position, and also Tierney's importance to the league champions, that is hardly a surprise.

"Kieran's going nowhere, he loves the football club," said his former captain Scott Brown on Sportsound.

"You never know what can happen, but I love watching the wee man play, I love his passion. When there's a 50-50 he wins it, when a ball goes into the box he puts his head on it.

"It's the quality on the other side as well. You can see why he went down to Arsenal. Other teams will want that, and Celtic are lucky to have these three [Tierney, McGregor and James Forrest] for that long a period."

Club captain McGregor is another who impressed in the league opener, but there's also been whispers that he might be on the way out. Those rumours seem to have died down in recent weeks.

"Callum has retired from Scotland so he's had the time off, and he looks really fresh," said Brown. "He is the brains of this time, he's got the understanding and leadership.

"If any young kids are watching, watch Callum McGregor, watch Kieran Tierney, watch James Forrest. You're not at a football club like this for that long if you can't understand the other side of the game."

title: Superb Short half-century guides Fire past Brave
description: Welsh Fire claim their fourth win in five matches in this season's Hundred as a well-crafted half-century from Matt Short helps them defeat Southern Brave by six wickets in Cardiff.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Sophia Gardens

Southern Brave 115-8 (100 balls): Stoinis 55 (39); Cook 3-14

Welsh Fire 116-4 (95 balls): Short 60* (41); Archer 2-19

Welsh Fire claimed their fourth win in five matches in this season's Hundred as a well-crafted half-century from Matt Short helped them defeat Southern Brave by six wickets in Cardiff.

Chasing 116, the home side lost captain Phil Salt early but a 56-run stand between Joe Root and Short provided them the platform to win on a tricky surface at Sophia Gardens.

Chris Jordan dismissed Root for 17 before Rachin Ravindra followed him for a duck to hand Brave hope of a way back into the contest.

Jordan Cox became the third Fire wicket to fall in the space of 10 runs but Short's composed innings ensured there was no collapse.

Still requiring more than a run a ball, Short scooped Jofra Archer for six to bring up his fifty from 37 balls before combining with Tom Kohler-Cadmore, who hit an unbeaten 23, to guide Fire over the line with five balls remaining.

Earlier, Brave endured a nightmare start after they were sent out to bat first as openers Jamie Smith and Ben McKinney were dismissed without opening their accounts.

With wickets falling around him regularly, Marcus Stoinis proved Brave's lone source of resistance against the Fire bowlers as the Australian all-rounder struck 55 from 39 balls before falling to Sam Cook, who returned figures of 3-14.

Nikhil Chaudhary struggled for his 18 and David Miller added 21 from 17 balls late on but no other Brave batter reached double figures as the visitors limped to 115-8.

While Fire moved level on 16 points with Trent Rockets at the top of the table, Brave remain fourth, with two wins, having played six matches.

Sunrisers Leeds face London Spirit at Headingley on Tuesday.

Both Sunrisers and Spirit will look for their second win of the season in the women's competition in the match starting at 15:00 BST, followed by the men's game at 18:30.
